match.reason: The closest bank point, leg-categories-crime, only lists offences against the person as one category among several and does not teach that each offence has elements the prosecution must prove, so it is broader than the new point.

draft.title: An offence against the person
card: An offence against the person harms, or threatens to harm, a person's body or life. Assault and homicide are examples.
Every offence has elements. These are the parts that make up the offence, and the prosecution must prove each one beyond reasonable doubt.
Most offences have two kinds of element: a physical act (the conduct) and a mental state (such as intending to cause harm, or being reckless about it).
If the prosecution cannot prove even one element, the accused is not guilty of that offence. The accused does not have to prove their innocence.
draft.remember: Offences against the person harm a body or a life, and the prosecution must prove every element.

a.q: Why must the prosecution prove the elements of an offence against the person?
opts: Each element is part of the offence, so all must be proved
Only the physical act needs proof, as the mind is assumed
The accused must prove the elements did not happen
The judge decides which elements are needed in each case
a.why: The elements make up the offence, so the prosecution must prove every one beyond reasonable doubt. The mental state is not assumed: it is an element too, and the burden never falls on the accused.
a.clue: Think about who has to prove guilt, and how much of it.

b.q: Dev is charged with an offence against the person. The prosecution proves he did the act, but the jury is not satisfied about his mental state. What is the likely outcome for that charge?
opts: Not guilty, as one element has not been proved
Guilty, as the physical act was proved
Guilty, unless Dev proves he lacked the mental state
A retrial, as the jury must find every element proved
b.why: Every element must be proved beyond reasonable doubt, and the mental state is an element. If the jury is not satisfied about it, Dev is not guilty of that offence. Proving the act alone is not enough.
b.clue: Does proving the act alone complete the offence?

a.best: Each element is part of the offence, so all must be proved

b.best: Not guilty, as one element has not been proved

problems.detail: The why says the burden "never" falls on the accused. The card only says the accused does not have to prove their innocence. In Victoria the accused can bear a burden for some defences, such as mental impairment, and for some statutory reverse-onus provisions. Limit it to the elements, e.g. "the accused does not have to prove the elements did not happen".

check.summary: Both questions are sound, with one clear right answer each. The only issue is a minor overstatement in why (a): the burden "never" falls on the accused, which is too absolute.
